Description: Ann Griffiths stated under cross-examination that her husband was subpoenaed as a witness for the prisoner, not for her.

Defense Strength: 0.9

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: When questioned about her sobriety, Ann Griffiths testified, 'I was not drunk.' She also claimed she was not so drunk that the Justice could not examine her.

Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: The mere fact that her sobriety is being questioned suggests it was an issue. Her denial is later contradicted by multiple witnesses.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: Isabella Macdaniel testified that Ann Griffiths threw half a brickbat at Gowens's head.

Prosecution Reasoning: This shows the victim engaged in serious violence, undermining her portrayal as a helpless victim of robbery.
Defense Strength: 1.0
Defense Reasoning: This evidence transforms the narrative from a robbery into a mutual, violent brawl. It demonstrates that the accuser was also an aggressor, making her claims of being a simple victim of theft highly suspect.

Description: William Cumming testified that on February 26th, around 10:30 PM, he was stopped by a group of 7-8 men he believed to be a press-gang. They surrounded and hustled him, and immediately after, he discovered his watch was missing from his pocket.

Description: Upon his arrest, prisoner Smith produced a paper stating he was authorized by a Mr. Whiteway to press men. Smith was described as the master of the gang.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: This corroborates the victim's initial belief that the attackers were a press-gang and places Smith as the leader of an organized group operating in the area.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: This could be interpreted as evidence of his occupation (a 'crimp'), not necessarily of his involvement in this specific robbery. It doesn't prove criminal intent.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: Sarah Willoughby, Smith's landlady, testified that Smith was at home very soon after ten o'clock on the Wednesday night of the robbery and did not go out again.
Prosecution Strength: 0.3

Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: Provides a direct alibi for Smith. If believed, it exonerates him completely.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: William Gilbert testified that the prisoner Ennis was at his house from about half past nine until about half past ten on the night of the robbery.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4

Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: Provides a direct alibi for Ennis from a seemingly credible witness, placing him away from the scene.

[EVIDENCE ev16]
Description: The victim, William Cumming, stated he did 'not know any thing of the other prisoner,' referring to Thomas Brewer. The only evidence linking Brewer was the watchman seeing him flee with Ennis.

Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: The primary witness and victim of the crime could not identify him, which is very strong evidence in his favor. His flight could have other explanations.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Christian Gayner, the prosecutor's wife, testified that on Monday morning, November 17th, she discovered a bed, bolster, and blankets were missing from a locked ground-floor room. She had last seen the items the previous night.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony establishes that a theft occurred from a specific, secured location at a specific time.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: This only establishes a theft occurred, but does not directly link it to the prisoner.

[EVIDENCE ev3]
Description: Mrs. Gayner positively identified the bed, blankets, and bolster recovered from the prisoner by the watchman as the property she had lost from her house.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This directly links the items found on the prisoner to the items stolen from the prosecutor's home, completing the chain of evidence for theft.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense does not contest the identity of the items, but rather how the prisoner came to possess them.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: Mrs. Gayner testified that the room from which the items were stolen was locked at 11 p.m. In the morning, she found the door half open with a different key in the lock, suggesting a break-in.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This evidence supports the charge of burglary, indicating that entry was forced or made with a false key, rather than through an open door.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: In a house with many lodgers, the security of any single room could be compromised by others, not necessarily the prisoner.

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: The prisoner's defense was that a man offered him one shilling to carry the bed, and that this man ran away when the watchman appeared.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a self-serving and uncorroborated story that fails to explain why the prisoner himself fled from the watchman.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: It provides an alternative, non-criminal explanation for his possession of the goods. Fleeing could be attributed to panic or fear of being wrongly implicated.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: Mrs. Gayner testified that the prisoner lodged in the house, on a different floor from where the theft occurred. This suggests he had legitimate access to the building's common areas.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: Proximity and access establish opportunity. He had no right to be in the specific locked room.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: As a lodger, his presence in the building was not inherently suspicious. It weakens the 'breaking and entering' element of burglary.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: James Kennedy, an officer, testified that although the house had two doors (one common to lodgers), it was legally considered a single dwelling house where the landlord resided, which is a requirement for a burglary charge.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This expert testimony clarifies a key legal point needed to sustain the burglary charge, countering potential defense arguments about the nature of the lodging house.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: The complexity of the house's layout (common passages, multiple doors) introduces reasonable doubt about whether the prisoner's actions constituted a 'breaking and entering' in the legal sense.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: The prisoner's uncle, Joseph Austin, testified that the prisoner was a shoemaker and he had never heard anything against his character before.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: Character testimony does not refute the direct evidence of being caught with the stolen goods.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: Positive character evidence from a family member suggests that criminal activity would be out of character for the prisoner.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: The prisoner's uncle also testified that Mrs. Gayner's house was 'full of bad women' and that the prisoner had been there with them.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony associates the prisoner with a disreputable environment and 'bad women,' potentially undermining his good character.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: This attempts to discredit the prosecutor's home as a place of ill repute, possibly suggesting a chaotic environment where property could be easily misplaced or taken by others.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: The final value of the stolen goods was assessed as 39 shillings, just under the threshold for a capital offense.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the value for the charge of grand larceny. The jury's verdict explicitly states this value.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The value is a matter of fact related to sentencing, not to whether the theft occurred.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Two other witnesses, aside from his uncle, were called and gave the prisoner a good character.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1

Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: Provides additional support for the prisoner's good character, suggesting the act was an anomaly or that he is being truthful.

Description: Valentine Labrow, the prosecutor, testified that the prisoner was his employee as a carpenter. He stated that a quantity of jalap went missing on July 18th, and part of it was subsequently found on the prisoner.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony establishes the core facts of the case: the defendant's access to the property, the theft of the goods, and the recovery of those goods from the defendant.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: While establishing the context, this testimony does not preclude an innocent explanation for how the prisoner came to possess the jalap.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: John Thomas, Mr. Labrow's shopman, testified that as the prisoner was leaving for the day, he observed his pockets were unusually bulky. This observation raised his suspicion.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This direct observation is what initiated the chain of events leading to the prisoner's capture and search. It provides a specific, suspicious behavior.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: Bulky pockets are not conclusive proof of theft and could have an innocent explanation. However, in the context of missing goods, it is highly suspicious.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: The prisoner's defense at trial was the statement, 'I picked it up after the things were taken away.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: The prosecution would argue this is a desperate, uncorroborated claim that is inconsistent with the prisoner's prior lies and his dramatic escape.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: This is the defendant's sole attempt to provide an innocent explanation for possessing the jalap. Its strength is extremely low given the other evidence.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Hugh Shepley, Esq., testified that he lost a large quantity of clothes from his bed-room. He stated he left his house on the 1st of December and returned on the 3rd to find the items missing.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony establishes that a significant theft occurred (the corpus delicti) and provides the timeframe for the crime.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The testimony does not, by itself, connect the prisoner to the crime.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: Lovett, an officer from Marlborough-street, testified that he apprehended the prisoner on the 2nd of December.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: The apprehension on December 2nd places the prisoner in the vicinity and timeframe of the crime, which occurred between December 1st and 3rd.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: The act of apprehension itself is not evidence of guilt for this specific crime.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: John Stinman, a publican, testified that the prisoner took a lodging at his house on December 3rd and brought in three large bundles the next day.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: The prisoner's acquisition of a large quantity of goods, packed in bundles, precisely coincides with the timing of the theft.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: This is consistent with the prisoner's claim that he purchased the goods in bulk on December 2nd.

[EVIDENCE ev10]
Description: David Myers, a tailor, testified that on December 7th, the prisoner brought him to his lodgings to sell him clothes. Myers bought two regimental jackets, coats, and breeches.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony from the buyer corroborates Stinman's account of the sale, confirming the prisoner's disposal of the goods.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: This is also consistent with the defense's claim of buying the goods to resell them.

[EVIDENCE ev14]
Description: The prisoner stated in his defense that he purchased all the articles on Monday, December 2nd, in Little St. James's-street. He claimed he saw a gentleman's servant bargaining with two Jews, outbid them by offering fifteen pounds, and bought the entire lot.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: The story is uncorroborated, as his alleged witness was not present, and it seems implausible given the circumstances.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: This is the defendant's sole explanation for being in possession of a large quantity of stolen goods. It offers an alternative, non-criminal narrative.

[EVIDENCE ev15]
Description: William-Michael Poppillow, a servant to Mr. Shepley, testified that he had seen the prisoner at Mr. Shepley's house in the kitchen on two or three occasions. He stated the prisoner used to visit the man servant.
Prosecution Strength: 1.0
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony is devastating to the defense. It establishes that the prisoner had prior knowledge of and access to the house, directly contradicting the implication of his defense that he was a stranger who acquired the goods elsewhere.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: Being at the house previously does not prove he committed the theft, but it strongly undermines his credibility.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Officer John Armstrong testified that on Feb 17th, he and other officers went to the prisoners' apartment. He found the main house door and the door to their room open. The prisoners, Pagett and Rothwell, were inside and were civil, with Pagett telling them, 'warrant or no warrant, you are welcome to search.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the prisoners' presence in the room where the counterfeiting materials were found.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: The open access to the room and their willing cooperation with the search suggest the prisoners had nothing to hide and that others could have placed the items there.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: In an armchair in the prisoners' room, Officer Armstrong found a leather bag containing 59 uncoloured counterfeit blanks the size of a shilling, along with 'sissil' (waste metal from which blanks are punched). He also found pliers, cork, sandpaper, file-dust, and six iron punches in the same area.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a comprehensive set of materials for manufacturing counterfeit coins, discovered in the prisoners' immediate presence.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense argued the items could belong to someone else, given the open access to the room mentioned in ev1.

[EVIDENCE ev3]
Description: Officer John Vickery testified that he found numerous counterfeit coins in the room. This included seven counterfeit sixpences in a tea caddie and a drawer containing counterfeit half guineas, seven-shilling pieces, shillings, and dollars. Some of these coins were described as 'fit for circulation.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: The presence of finished coins, in addition to the manufacturing materials, indicates a functioning and successful counterfeiting operation was taking place in the apartment.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense's position is that these items, like the tools, were not the prisoners'.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: Officer Daniel Bishop found a vial of vitriol and, hidden under rags and a washing-tub, a vial containing aqua fortis. Bishop, a former dyer, testified he was certain the substance was aqua fortis from its taste and his decade of experience using it.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Aqua fortis is the key chemical needed for 'colouring' base metal with silver, the specific crime charged. Its discovery, and the apparent attempt to hide it, is very strong evidence.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense questioned Bishop's expertise as he was not a chemist, suggesting the identification could be wrong or the chemical was for another purpose.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: During the search of the apartment, Officer Armstrong heard Elizabeth Pagett say, 'take care of my goods,' in reference to the items in the room.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This statement is an admission of ownership over the room's contents, including the counterfeiting materials. It specifically implicates Pagett.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The statement could be interpreted as a general remark about her legitimate personal belongings, not necessarily an admission regarding the illegal items.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Officer Armstrong testified that during the search, James Rothwell remarked that 'he was unlucky that he had just come up.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This statement could be interpreted as an admission of guilt, implying he was unlucky to be caught in the act or during a police raid.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This statement is highly ambiguous and could equally mean he was unlucky to be visiting at the exact moment of a police raid, without implying any involvement.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: The landlady, Eleanor Bromage, testified that she had let the apartment to Elizabeth Pagett and another woman. She stated that Rothwell did not live there, but was merely a visitor whom she had seen there on occasion.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: The testimony still places Rothwell at the location, but weakens the prosecution's ability to tie him directly to the items.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This is crucial exculpatory evidence for Rothwell, establishing that he was not the tenant and had no permanent connection to the room or its contents. This makes his claim of non-involvement highly plausible.

[EVIDENCE ev10]
Description: During the cross-examination of Officer Armstrong, the defense established that no files were found during the search. The defense counsel suggested that files were a necessary instrument for preparing the blanks and making the tools complete.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a minor point if other evidence of a coining operation is strong.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This suggests the set of tools for counterfeiting was incomplete, which could be used to argue that no active operation was underway or that the materials were for some other purpose.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: In her defense, Elizabeth Pagett stated, 'I am innocent of the charge that is laid against me.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.0
Prosecution Reasoning: A standard denial of guilt from a defendant.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: This is a standard denial, but its credibility is significantly weakened by her status as the tenant, her claim of ownership of the room's contents, and her earlier false statement about the aqua fortis.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: The prosecutor, John Wells, testified that his premises included a shop and dwelling area, part of which was occupied by another tenant, Octavius Bradley. The section where the theft occurred was part of Wells's shop, separated by a partition.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the location of the crime and its connection to a dwelling, which is necessary for the burglary charge.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: Introduces ambiguity about the nature of the premises, as part of it was occupied by another person and separated, which could be argued against it being a single dwelling house.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: John Wells stated that on the night of the incident, no person slept in his part of the premises. The prisoner, his apprentice, had not slept there for a year.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This fact is detrimental to the prosecution's primary charge of burglary, which legally requires the targeted location to be an occupied dwelling-house.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This is a very strong point for the defense, as it directly undermines a key element of the burglary charge. The jury ultimately agreed, convicting on the lesser charge of theft.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: The morning after the incident, Wells found the shop door ajar. Harris, upon arriving, denied leaving it open and insisted he had double-locked it the previous night.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: Harris's firm denial, which is contradicted by other evidence, suggests he is lying to cover his involvement.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: Harris's statement could be interpreted as genuine confusion or a mistaken belief, not necessarily a lie.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: John Stantiford, a porter, testified that he was standing against the shop door from ten until nearly a quarter to eleven and believed it to be fast, though he did not physically try it.
Prosecution Strength: 0.3
Prosecution Reasoning: The witness's belief is not certain, as he admits he did not try the door. The timeframe also leaves a window for the crime to occur after he left.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This suggests the shop was secure during a significant portion of the alleged timeframe of the burglary, making it less likely that an opportunistic crime occurred.

[EVIDENCE ev15]
Description: John Wells testified that Harris had worked for him 'on and off for five years' and there was 'no dependance upon him.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This character evidence suggests the prisoner was unreliable, which may make him seem more likely to have committed the crime in the eyes of the jury.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: This is subjective character testimony from the victim and could be seen as biased. Being unreliable is not the same as being a thief.

[EVIDENCE ev16]
Description: In his defense, the prisoner stated, 'It is my first crime that I have committed, and I hope you will have a little mercy.'
Prosecution Strength: 1.0
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a clear admission of guilt. The prisoner does not contest the facts but instead pleads for mercy, confirming his culpability for the theft.
Defense Strength: 0.0
Defense Reasoning: This statement effectively ends any defense against the charge of theft, shifting the focus entirely to sentencing and mitigation.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: Jordan claimed that her husband's handkerchief went missing from the tester of the bed on a Sunday. She stated she asked Dillon about it half an hour later, and Dillon denied any knowledge of it.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This provides a specific timeline for the theft and shows the defendant had an early opportunity to return the item but denied having it.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: This testimony depends entirely on Jordan's account of events, which is later shown to be unreliable.

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: Dillon stated in her defense that she 'did not think it was her handkerchief' and 'thought some of the people had dropped it, so I picked it up.' This contradicts the claim of a confession.
Prosecution Strength: 0.3
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a self-serving denial that directly contradicts the prosecutrix's testimony about a confession.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: This provides an alternative, innocent explanation for possessing the handkerchief, which becomes more plausible as the prosecutrix's credibility fails.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: The constable, John Wygate, testified that he searched the prisoner's box and found the ring, but he did not see any money.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: Finding the ring offers some corroboration, but the absence of the money weakens a significant part of the theft charge.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: The failure to find the stolen money casts doubt on the entire accusation, especially the most valuable part of the alleged theft.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Mary Macartney, a lodger, testified that she was present during a search of Dillon's box and saw both the handkerchief and the money.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony corroborates Jordan's claim that the stolen items were in the box, adding a second witness.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: While supporting the prosecution initially, her testimony leads to the unraveling of the prosecutrix's primary narrative.

[EVIDENCE ev13]
Description: Jordan admitted she could not swear the money was hers and stated it was returned to her by an acquaintance who was not present in court to testify.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony is based on hearsay and the witness's own admission of uncertainty, making it very weak evidence.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: The prosecution fails to prove ownership of the money, which is a key element of the charge, effectively nullifying this part of the indictment.

[EVIDENCE ev14]
Description: Dillon's defense regarding the money was that it was her own, left to her by her husband who had gone abroad.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a plausible but uncorroborated claim by the defendant.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: Given the prosecution's failure to identify the money (ev13), this innocent explanation becomes credible.

[EVIDENCE ev15]
Description: Jordan testified that when Dillon started her service, she needed seventeen shillings to get her property out of pawn, which Jordan advanced to her.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes a potential financial motive for the defendant to steal.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: While it shows a need for money, it does not prove theft. It could also show a relationship of trust where the employer was willing to help.

[EVIDENCE ev16]
Description: Jordan confirmed that 'some trifle' of wages were due to Dillon when she left the service.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: The amount was a 'trifle,' suggesting it would not alleviate any significant financial distress.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This slightly weakens the argument that Dillon was in such desperate need of money that she would resort to theft.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: The party of deserters, including the deceased Timothy Kirby, halted without orders at Barnet. They stated they were unable to continue to Highgate without refreshment, having had none since noon the previous day.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes the context of the soldiers' desperation and fatigue, suggesting the Sergeant's subsequent actions were disproportionately cruel.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This evidence demonstrates that the deserters were insubordinate and refusing a direct order to march, providing context for the need to restore discipline.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: According to civilian witness Matthew Smith, as Sgt. Mack raised his halbert to strike the fatal blow, he said, 'I will murder you, you b-r.'
Prosecution Strength: 1.0
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a direct statement of murderous intent made at the moment of the act, providing powerful evidence for the charge of wilful murder.
Defense Strength: 0.0
Defense Reasoning: The defense cannot easily refute this testimony from an independent civilian witness.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: Surgeons who examined Kirby confirmed that an instrument had penetrated his skull and entered the brain. The surgeon who performed the post-mortem had 'no doubt at all' that this wound was the cause of death.
Prosecution Strength: 1.0
Prosecution Reasoning: This medically establishes the link between the blow and the death, fulfilling a necessary component of the murder charge.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: The defense does not dispute the cause of death, but argues about the intent and circumstances leading to it.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Civilian eyewitnesses Thomas Webb and Matthew Smith both testified that Kirby had made no physical threat or motion to strike Sgt. Mack before the blow was delivered. Smith stated any such claim was 'a very false thing.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Testimony from independent civilians directly contradicts the defense's claim of self-defense, making it appear fabricated.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense relies on its own witnesses to counter this, suggesting the civilians may not have seen everything.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Officer Wiltshire, who had received Mack as a volunteer from the militia, testified that he came with 'an exceeding good character' and that in his experience, 'he has always behaved well; I never found him inhuman.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: Character evidence does not negate the specific facts of the case, especially the numerous threats.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: Positive character testimony from a commanding officer suggests that the violent act was out of character and more likely the result of provocation or accident than malice.

[EVIDENCE ev13]
Description: Under cross-examination, escort soldier Thomas Wilson admitted that his reason for believing Mack only meant to strike with the wooden part of the halbert was because Mack had told him so after the incident.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This undermines a key part of the defense's argument about intent, revealing it to be based on the defendant's self-serving statement rather than the witness's direct observation.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense is weakened as this suggests the soldiers' stories might be coordinated or influenced by the defendant.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Elizabeth Ibbett, wife of the property owner, testified that on Sunday, March 2nd, she and her husband left for a funeral, leaving the prisoner, Edward Basset, as the only person in the room. When they returned, they discovered three blankets and a sheet were missing from his bed.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony establishes that the items went missing during a period when the defendant had exclusive opportunity to take them.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: This relies on the witness's claim that the defendant was the *only* person left, which the defendant disputes.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: Elizabeth Castletine, a neighbor who lived opposite the lodging house, testified that she saw Basset come down the stairs with a bundle on the afternoon of the incident. She stated, 'I saw something like a blanket, there were holes in the bag.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is direct eyewitness testimony that places the defendant leaving the scene with a bundle containing items that match the description of the stolen goods.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: The witness could not definitively identify the contents of the bag, only that it was 'something like a blanket'.

[EVIDENCE ev3]
Description: Patrick Mackcaller, who lodged in the same room, testified that he saw Basset come into the room 'of a bustle and went to the cupboard, after that he went to his box, and took something out,' although he did not know what it was.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony suggests hurried and potentially suspicious activity by the defendant in the room around the time of the theft.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The witness did not see what was taken, and the actions described are not inherently incriminating.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: Mrs. Ibbett testified that when the defendant returned to his lodgings on the night of the incident, 'he did not ask after the blankets.' He was arrested the following night.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: An innocent person would likely inquire about their missing bedding. The failure to do so suggests knowledge of what happened to them.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: The defendant may have had other reasons for not asking, and this is circumstantial evidence regarding his state of mind.

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: During cross-examination, Mrs. Ibbett confirmed that Basset had lodged with her for six to eight months and had always paid his rent regularly.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: Past good behavior does not preclude the commission of a crime.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: This establishes the defendant's good character as a reliable and honest tenant, making theft seem less probable.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: Mrs. Ibbett stated that the room contained four beds and that seven people slept in it, although the prisoner 'mostly had a bed to himself' at that time.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: This does not change the fact that he was allegedly the only one present at the time of the theft.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: This evidence suggests that multiple other people had access to the room and its contents, introducing reasonable doubt and alternative suspects.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Mrs. Ibbett testified that the defendant 'complained in the middle of the night that he was cold.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: This could be interpreted as an indirect admission, as he would be cold if he no longer had his blankets.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This is the action of a victim suffering from the loss of his blankets, not a thief trying to conceal a crime.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: James Murray testified that the prisoner came to his house for tea around 3 p.m. on the day of the incident and stayed with him until 10 p.m. that night.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1

Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This provides a strong, corroborated alibi for the majority of the time when the theft could have occurred.

Prosecution Strength: 0.0
Prosecution Reasoning: General character does not prove innocence of a specific charge.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: Positive character testimony makes it less likely that the defendant would engage in criminal behavior such as theft.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Samuel James testified that on the evening of November 1st in Hyde Park, the prisoner, Watkin Herbert, passed him, turned around, kicked his heels, and struck him, causing him to fall on his back. The prisoner then demanded his property.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is the victim's direct testimony establishing the core elements of a violent robbery: assault, fear, and a demand for property.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense disputes this narrative, claiming the encounter was consensual and did not involve a robbery. However, this is the primary account of the crime.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: James testified that among the stolen items was a £10 bank note he had received that day for his wages. He stated that his master's scribe always wrote the name 'Richard Fitzgeorge Stackfold' on his bank notes.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This provides a specific, unique, and falsifiable detail about the stolen property, which can be used for later identification.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: At this point in the testimony, this is an uncorroborated claim. The defense could suggest the detail was invented.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: William Gibbons, a soldier in the same regiment, testified that he was on sentry duty and saw Herbert 'run into the barracks' about twenty minutes before Samuel James arrived to report the robbery.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This places Herbert arriving hastily at the barracks shortly after the time of the robbery and just before it was reported, which is highly suspicious.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: Running into the barracks before roll call is not inherently a criminal act and could be coincidental.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: In his defense, Herbert claimed that he met James, who made a homosexual proposition to him ('he says had you ever any connection with a man') and voluntarily gave him the bank note to persuade him.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: This is an uncorroborated, self-serving alternative narrative that attempts to re-frame the encounter. It is undermined by Herbert's subsequent admission of using force.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: This provides the only alternative explanation for possessing the note. If believed, it would negate the charge of robbery, even if it admits to a lesser crime.

The prosecution alleges that the defendants, along with an accomplice who turned King's evidence, committed the murder during a footpad robbery.

public.prior_belief: Prior: equal probability of guilt and innocence before evidence examination.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Thomas Meyer, the victim's brother-in-law, testified that Mr. Steele left London on November 5th, 1802, for his property in Feltham. After Mr. Steele failed to return, Meyer initiated a search on Hounslow Heath.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the victim's identity, his presence near the crime scene, and the timeline of his disappearance, providing the foundation for the murder charge.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: This testimony does not connect the defendants to the crime in any way.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: Benjamin Hanfield, an accomplice granted a pardon, testified that John Holloway approached him to commit a 'footpad robbery'. Hanfield stated Holloway identified Owen Haggerty as the third conspirator, and they all met at the Black Horse pub before heading to Hounslow Heath.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is direct testimony implicating both defendants in the premeditation of the robbery that led to the murder.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: The testimony comes from an accomplice with a criminal past who is testifying to save himself, making his credibility highly questionable.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: John Smith, a coachman, testified that on the night of the murder, as his coach passed between the trees and the eleven-mile stone on Hounslow Heath, he heard a man groan twice. He stated the first groan was louder and the second was more faint.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This is powerful independent corroboration of a specific and unusual detail in Hanfield's testimony: the two groans and the passing of a heavy coach.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: The witness did not see anything, and hearing groans on a heath at night is not definitive proof of this specific crime.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: Multiple witnesses, including officers and publicans, testified that Holloway, Haggerty, and Hanfield were frequently seen in each other's company at pubs in the Dyot Street area around the time of the murder.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes a clear association between the three men, making the conspiracy described by Hanfield plausible and directly contradicting the defendants' initial denials.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: Proves only association, not conspiracy to murder.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Magistrate John Nares testified that both defendants made false statements during their examinations. Haggerty denied knowing Hanfield and gave a false alibi of working for a Mr. Smith, which Smith refuted. Holloway also denied being at Hounslow and provided several false work alibis that were disproven by the named employers.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Demonstrates consciousness of guilt. The defendants told multiple, verifiable lies about their associations and whereabouts, suggesting they had something to hide.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defendants could be lying out of fear or confusion. Holloway claimed he made a mistake about the year of his employment.

[EVIDENCE ev13]
Description: Officer Daniel Bishop testified that he overheard conversations between Holloway and Haggerty in their separate lock-up rooms. They discussed Hanfield's testimony and the lies they had told the magistrate (e.g., Holloway: "I denied it entirely..."; Haggerty: "So did I."), but at no point did they protest their innocence to each other.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is strong evidence of shared knowledge and guilt. Their private conversation focused on the strength of the evidence and their cover story, not on any actual claim of innocence, implying they were co-conspirators.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The conversation could be interpreted as two innocent men discussing how to combat a false accusation, though the specific content makes this explanation weak.

[EVIDENCE ev15]
Description: Under cross-examination, Hanfield admitted to a life of crime, stating he got his living 'Sometimes by thieving and sometimes by industry.' He also stated his confession was due to 'compunction of conscience,' despite four years of silence and the existence of a reward.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: His character admission weakens the prosecution's case which relies heavily on his testimony.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: This evidence severely undermines the credibility of the prosecution's star witness, suggesting his testimony may be fabricated to secure a pardon and reward money.

Description: Officer Daniel Cartwright testified that upon apprehending the prisoner, he searched him and found seven pounds in bank notes and two canvas bags.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: While the money is circumstantial, possession of large canvas bags is suspicious and connects to Barton's testimony (ev3).
Defense Strength: 0.5

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Defense witness Samuel Bagley, a shoemaker, testified that he met the prisoner in Lime-street on the morning of Wednesday, April 8th. He saw Lovett working as a porter, helping a gentleman with a load into a hackney coach.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: The defendant William Singleton was employed as a footman by the victim, Mr. Rawlinson, on May 13th. The stolen plate was placed under his particular care, so much so that he requested a list of it upon starting his service.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes that Singleton had both access and responsibility for the stolen items, demonstrating clear means and opportunity.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: These are undisputed facts of his employment and do not directly prove theft.

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: When Mr. Rawlinson and officers first visited Richard Thompson's hairdressing shop, Thompson denied knowing any servant by the name of 'Dench' (Singleton's alias) and claimed he had 'no transaction of that kind'.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This denial, later proven false by other evidence, suggests consciousness of guilt and an attempt to deceive investigators.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: Thompson might genuinely not have known the alias or could have been cautious when questioned about criminal matters.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: During a search of Richard Thompson at his shop, officers found five silver tea spoons in his coat pocket. Mr. Rawlinson identified the spoons as his property by their crest and a unique polisher's mark.
Prosecution Strength: 1.0
Prosecution Reasoning: This is direct physical evidence linking Thompson to the stolen goods, making him a receiver of stolen property.
Defense Strength: 0.0
Defense Reasoning: Possession of positively identified stolen property is exceptionally difficult to explain away innocently.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: A pawn ticket for a soup ladle was found in the pocket of Thompson's wife. A pawnbroker confirmed Thompson's wife pledged the ladle, which Mr. Rawlinson believed was his, though he could not positively swear to it.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This links Thompson's household to another piece of the stolen property, suggesting a pattern of receiving and disposing of the goods.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense could argue that Thompson's wife acted independently and he had no knowledge. The identification of the ladle was also not positive.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Ann Hardest, a cook from Singleton's previous employer, testified that Richard Thompson had visited Singleton there, establishing a prior acquaintance between the two men.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony makes Singleton's claim that he went to Thompson for help more plausible, as it shows they knew each other before the crime.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: This merely proves they were acquainted, not that they were co-conspirators.

[EVIDENCE ev14]
Description: Singleton's defense called four witnesses who gave him a good character.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: Character evidence is generally weak in the face of strong factual evidence like a confession and exclusive opportunity.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: This evidence suggests that committing such a crime would be out of character for Singleton, which may raise doubt for the jury.

[EVIDENCE ev15]
Description: Mr. Rawlinson stated that when he hired Singleton, he did so based on a 'good character from major - , as to honesty and sobriety.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This has minimal impact on the prosecution's case.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: This corroborates the defense's claim of good character, coming from the victim himself, which adds weight to the idea the act was uncharacteristic.

Description: Justinian Casanager testified that a spring table clock was taken from his house in Potterhill, Hertfordshire. He first became aware of its location when he saw it at the Marlborough-street office.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Elizabeth Sibley, the prosecutor, testified that she went out around 4 PM, having locked her room door with a padlock. She stated she was certain she had locked it because it was her custom and a thing she never failed to do.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the room was secured, implying a forced entry was necessary which is central to the burglary charge. Her certainty adds weight to this claim.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense can argue her certainty is based on habit rather than a specific memory of the event, leaving room for doubt.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: Mrs. Sibley testified that around 8 PM, the prisoner, who was a lodger in the same house, approached her at a local pub and told her, 'you have left your door open.' Sibley denied this, stating she was sure she had locked it.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: This can be interpreted as the prisoner attempting to create a false narrative or alibi that the door was unsecured, pointing towards his guilt and premeditation.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This supports the defense's claim of an ongoing interaction and dispute between the parties. It shows they were in contact that evening, which is consistent with the defense's story.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: Sibley testified that on the Sunday before the incident, the prisoner had been at her room door and saw where she took a silver spoon from when she opened the drawer to lend him one.
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes that the prisoner had prior knowledge of the valuables and their specific location, suggesting he had the opportunity and information to commit the crime.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: This could be framed as a normal, innocent interaction between a landlady and lodger, not a preparatory act for theft.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: The pawnbroker, Mr. Grindel, testified that he believed the watch had been previously pledged with him by Mrs. Sibley herself. This contradicted Sibley's statement that she had never pledged any of the items.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This severely undermines the credibility of the prosecution's sole witness, suggesting she committed perjury.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This is extremely strong evidence for the defense. It demonstrates that the prosecutrix lied under oath, making her entire testimony, including the accusation of theft, unreliable.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: Officer William Hewit testified that he found two silver seals belonging to the watch in the prisoner's breeches pocket. These seals had been removed from the watch and were not pawned with the other items.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This action strongly suggests personal appropriation rather than pawning on behalf of another. If he was acting for Sibley, there would be no reason to separate the seals and hide them in his pocket.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense has no good explanation for this. It significantly weakens the claim that he was merely acting as an agent for Sibley.

[EVIDENCE ev16]
Description: The pawnbroker, Mr. Grindel, when asked about Sibley's house, testified, 'I have heard that girls lived there.' The Court interpreted this as evidence of it being a 'disorderly house.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony from a third party damages the reputation and credibility of the prosecution's main witness.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: Provides independent corroboration for the defendant's accusation (ev14), supporting his narrative that the prosecutrix is of bad character and therefore untrustworthy.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: Thomas Oldfield testified that during the struggle, he got the robber on the ground and 'struck him a very large blow on the nose.' This happened after the robber pulled out a bayonet.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony provides a direct cause for the physical injuries later observed on the prisoner.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense does not directly contest the struggle but offers an alternative cause for the injuries.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: The victim testified that the robber produced a bayonet during their struggle, which the victim managed to seize and later turned over to an officer.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: The recovery of the weapon provides a critical piece of physical evidence linking the crime to its owner.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense does not contest that a bayonet was involved but claims it was stolen from the prisoner.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Witness John Lane testified that when Corporal Bell and the victim were approaching his house to find Walker, the prisoner 'went towards my back door' before Lane told him to 'stand your ground.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This action is indicative of a consciousness of guilt and an attempt to flee upon seeing the authorities.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense could argue the prisoner was simply startled or afraid for other reasons, though the context makes this unlikely.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: The victim, Thomas Oldfield, admitted under questioning that he 'drank part of three pints of wine' before the incident but insisted, 'I was quite sober.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.5
Prosecution Reasoning: By admitting to drinking but maintaining sobriety, the witness appears candid while upholding the reliability of his testimony.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: The admission of consuming a significant amount of alcohol allows the defense to question the victim's perception, memory, and judgment during the event.

[EVIDENCE ev10]
Description: Five witnesses were called for the defense and 'gave him a good character.' One witness, John Lane, also stated that during the nine or ten weeks he knew Walker, he 'worked hard' and 'behaved exceeding well.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: Good character does not negate the facts of a specific crime. The judge even instructed the jury that it 'ought not to operate upon your verdict.'
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: Strong character evidence suggests the alleged crime would be out of character, which can raise reasonable doubt. It was compelling enough for the jury and prosecutor to recommend mercy.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: The victim testified that the robbery occurred on a 'Very moon light' night.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes that visibility was good, which supports the credibility and accuracy of the victim's visual identification of the robber.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense cannot easily dispute the weather conditions, though they can still argue that identification was difficult.

[EVIDENCE ev_pl_01]
Description: The prosecutor, Richard Jones, testified that he and his partner were soap manufacturers and that the prisoner, Patrick Long, was a laborer in their manufactory.

[EVIDENCE ev_pl_11]

Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: This provides the sole alternative explanation for his possession of soap, forming the entirety of his defense. However, its credibility is very low given the other evidence.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Joseph Covington testified that on April 1st, he left his room securely fastened with three locks. Upon his return on May 1st, he found the locks broken and all his property, valued at around £120, stolen.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes that a burglary and significant theft occurred, providing the basis for the charges.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: This fact does not identify the perpetrators and is neutral as to their identity.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: Corcoran admitted under cross-examination that he was arrested as the thief and only told his story after being taken into custody.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: The prosecution can only argue that he told the truth once apprehended.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: Provides a strong motive for Corcoran to fabricate a story to shift blame and save himself, severely damaging his credibility.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Mary Chiswell, a landlady, testified that James Westbrook and Elizabeth Phipps came to lodge with her on April 2nd, the day after the robbery, using the false name 'James Smith'.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Using a false name immediately after a crime is strong evidence of consciousness of guilt. This evidence is independent of Corcoran's testimony.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense could argue there are other reasons for using a false name, although it is highly suspicious.

[EVIDENCE ev10]
Description: Officer Limbric found a chisel in Covington's house that matched the pry marks on a forced drawer.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: Suggests the tool used for the break-in, but does not directly link it to the defendants, only that it was found at the scene.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: The chisel was found in the house, not on the defendants. It could have belonged to anyone or been left by the true culprit.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: Elizabeth Phipps claimed in her defense that the Covingtons dealt in stolen property and had given her items, and that the goods moved were her own property.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: Her story is self-serving and lacks any corroborating evidence, appearing as a desperate attempt to create doubt.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: Offers an alternative explanation for possessing the goods, however improbable and unsupported.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Ann Price testified that Samuel Westbrook, who was accused of assisting, was at home working all morning on the day of the robbery.
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony only pertains to one of the four defendants and does not address the actions of Westbrook and Phipps.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: Provides a strong alibi for Samuel, which directly contradicts a key part of Corcoran's testimony about the bundle transfer.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: John Morgan, the prosecutor, testified that he left the prisoners, Wharton and Hutton, to conduct his business in his Bond-street shop while he went to Hastings on August 19th.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the prisoners had custody of and access to the goods, which is a necessary precondition for the theft.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: Establishes the context for the defense's claim that they were acting under Morgan's instructions.

[EVIDENCE ev3]
Description: Morgan testified that Wharton came to him in Hastings and proposed a plan to feign bankruptcy and conceal goods, stating that 'eight hundred pounds might be put in my pocket.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.7
Prosecution Reasoning: Paints Wharton as the originator of a criminal conspiracy, establishing his dishonest character and motive.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: The defense claims this conversation happened, but that Morgan initiated and agreed to the plan, not Wharton. It confirms a conspiracy was discussed.

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: Wharton wrote a letter to Morgan on September 14th, stating, 'Our shop has been robbed of nearly every thing that is in it'.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: The prosecution presents this as a lie written by a thief to cover his tracks after stealing the goods.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: The defense claims this letter was part of the pre-arranged plan with Morgan to create the illusion of a robbery for the benefit of creditors.

[EVIDENCE ev6]
Description: The indicted goods (Irish linen, tablecloths, etc.) were found in a trunk belonging to the prisoner Wharton, which was discovered in the bedroom he shared with Hutton.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is strong physical evidence directly linking the prisoner Wharton to the missing goods, which were found packed in his personal trunk.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: The defense's explanation is that packing goods into trunks was part of the concealment plan agreed to with Morgan. It requires believing their entire narrative.

[EVIDENCE ev7]
Description: Morgan admitted under cross-examination that he started his business with 'none whatever' capital and had bills becoming due to the amount of £3,500, with not 'a single hundred to take them up with.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This fact is very damaging to the prosecution's case as it establishes a powerful motive for Morgan to defraud his creditors.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This provides a strong motive for Morgan to concoct the scheme Wharton described, lending significant credibility to the defense's entire story.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: John Perks, the officer, testified that upon examining the premises after the reported robbery, he 'could not discover that any forcible entry had been made, either outside or inside.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.3
Prosecution Reasoning: The prosecution's case is that it was an inside job by the employees who had keys, so a lack of forced entry is not inconsistent with their theory.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: The lack of forced entry is highly consistent with a staged robbery, where no actual break-in occurred. It undermines the idea of an external robbery.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: Sowerby testified that Morgan only told him about the authority to pawn goods after a large quantity of pawned items were discovered, and that Morgan's explanation of a £60 limit seemed 'very disproportionate' to the amount of goods found.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: This is very damaging to Morgan's credibility. It suggests he was inventing an explanation post-facto to account for the discovered goods.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This testimony from a neutral creditor strongly implies Morgan was being deceptive and that his story about the limited pawning authority was not truthful, lending weight to the defense's claims of a larger plot.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Sowerby stated that he and the other creditors initially instituted the prosecution, but 'in consequence of what you have since learned you have dropped it, and left Mr. Morgan to go on with it.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This fact is extremely damaging to the prosecution. It shows that the parties who were actually being defrauded (the creditors) no longer believed Wharton was the primary culprit.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: This is powerful evidence suggesting the creditors, after hearing both sides, came to believe Wharton's version of events—that Morgan was the one trying to defraud them. Their abandonment of the case validates the defense's core claim.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Samuel Taunton, a Bow-street officer, testified that on March 1st, he went to Miss Brodrick's house to apprehend the prisoner, George White, with a warrant for sedition.
Prosecution Strength: 0.3
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the context for the officer's presence but is not directly related to the theft charge. The initial reason for the arrest (sedition) is separate from the discovery of the stolen wine.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: The defense could argue the officer's search was pretextual and that the sedition charge, of which nothing more is mentioned, suggests a potential bias against the prisoner.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: Officer Taunton identified two of the bottles found in the drawer as Cape wine.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This specific detail becomes crucial when combined with Miss Brodrick's testimony that she never gave the prisoner Cape wine.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The defense has no good counter to this fact, other than to deny the wine was Cape wine, which is not attempted.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: Miss Brodrick testified that the prisoner had been her butler for about seven weeks.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes that the prisoner was in a position of trust and had access to and knowledge of the house, including the location of the wine cellar.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: This fact is neutral on its own but is necessary for the prosecution's narrative of an inside job.

[EVIDENCE ev10]
Description: Miss Brodrick stated she keeps her wine in an inner cellar, for which she holds the only key, and delivers out specific quantities to the butler.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony establishes a system of control over the wine stock, suggesting that any wine not officially delivered out would have to be taken illicitly.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The defense could question the infallibility of this system, but it presents a strong case for controlled access.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Miss Brodrick believed the amount of Sherry and Port in the outer cellar was consistent with what she had given him for consumption, minus what had been used.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: This suggests the prisoner was stealing specific, likely more valuable or less-used wines from the inner cellar, while maintaining the appearance of properly managing the everyday wine stock.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: The defense could argue this shows he was an honest butler managing his stocks correctly, and that her assessment of the quantity was only 'nearly so'.

[EVIDENCE ev13]
Description: Miss Brodrick testified that upon examining her cellar, she missed twenty-four quarts and six pints of wine.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This confirms a theft has occurred and quantifies the loss. It provides the corpus delicti (the body of the crime).
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: While this proves a theft, it doesn't solely point to the prisoner. However, combined with other evidence, it becomes very strong.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Hannah Lawrence testified that the prisoner, introducing himself as Thomas Scott, agreed to purchase her furniture. He paid part in cash and offered two bills of exchange for the remainder, one of which was for £19 14s.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes the initial transaction and the prisoner's use of the alias 'Thomas Scott' to obtain goods on credit.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: The description of a standard commercial transaction, on its own, does not prove fraudulent intent.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: James Reeves, the clerk at Union Hall, testified that when the prisoner was brought in, he gave his name as Thomas Bontein.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: Officially establishes the prisoner's identity as Thomas Bontein in this legal context, corroborating the witnesses who identified him under that name.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: Does not preclude him from having also used the name 'Scott'.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: Officer James Glannon testified that he found a certificate of discharge under the insolvent act in the prisoner's lodging, which bore the name 'Bontein'.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: Provides physical evidence linking the prisoner to the name Thomas Bontein, further weakening the idea that 'Scott' was his only or primary identity.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: Consistent with the defense that he used multiple names, but does not prove the use of 'Scott' was fraudulent.

[EVIDENCE ev10]
Description: Defense witness William Thomas Allen testified that he knew the prisoner in 1810 continually by the name of Thomas Scott and never by any other name, though he had nicknames like 'Bout' and 'Bontein'.
Prosecution Strength: 0.3
Prosecution Reasoning: The mention of 'Bontein' as a nickname weakens the claim that he was *only* known as Scott, suggesting the names were interchangeable or aliases.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: This is the primary evidence for the defense, suggesting 'Thomas Scott' was a legitimate name the prisoner used for business, not a forgery.

public.sender_utility: Prosecution utility: highest for convicting guilty defendants properly, positive for proper procedures, negative for wrongful convictions or dismissed cases due to improper methods.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: Simon Bathgate testified that he was in the Marquis of Granby public-house with two men. During a purported demonstration of a gambling trick, one of the men took his £10 note out of his hand, claimed to have won it, and handed it to the other man.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony establishes that a crime—the theft of the £10 note—occurred in the manner described.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: While it describes a crime, this testimony alone does not link the prisoner, Charles Wheeler, to the event, as the victim was unable to identify him.

[EVIDENCE ev2]
Description: When asked to identify the second man involved in the trick, Simon Bathgate stated, 'I cannot positively say whether it was the prisoner or not. ... I do not recollect the man.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a significant failure in the prosecution's case, as the direct victim cannot identify the defendant as one of the perpetrators.
Defense Strength: 0.9
Defense Reasoning: The victim's inability to identify the prisoner creates substantial reasonable doubt about his involvement.

[EVIDENCE ev3]
Description: Simon Bathgate testified that he was 'perfectly certain' of the other man, identifying him as James Wheeler, the prisoner's brother who was previously tried for the offense.
Prosecution Strength: 0.6
Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes a connection between the crime and the Wheeler family, making the prisoner's involvement more plausible by association.
Defense Strength: 0.4
Defense Reasoning: This evidence pertains to the prisoner's brother, not the prisoner himself. The guilt of one brother does not prove the guilt of the other.

[EVIDENCE ev4]
Description: James Hodges, a beadle, testified that around one o'clock on November 24th, he saw the prisoner, Charles Wheeler, and his brother James coming out of the Marquis of Granby public-house.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This testimony from an officer of the court places the prisoner at the scene of the crime at the exact time it occurred, corroborating other evidence.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: Being present at a location does not prove commission of a crime.

[EVIDENCE ev8]
Description: John Rose, a clerk at Messrs. Barclay's, testified that the prosecutor reported the lost note. About half an hour later, a young woman brought the note to be changed, and he detained it.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: This shows that the stolen note was quickly put into circulation by an associate of the thieves, which is consistent with the crime.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: The person who presented the note was a young woman, not the prisoner, providing no direct link.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1_body_found]
Description: The body of a man, later identified as Edward Clifford, was found in a pond in a brick-field. The body had 'great cuts on the side of the head,' indicating a violent death.

Prosecution Reasoning: This establishes the corpus delicti, proving that a murder has occurred and initiating the investigation.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: While this confirms a death, it does not in itself implicate the defendant, James Leary.

[EVIDENCE ev8_leary_incriminating_statement]
Description: Officer Thisselton and Thomas M'Carthy testified that Leary, while in custody, stated that if he could get someone to prove he was in bed at 10 o'clock 'it would be all right,' but admitted 'that is where I should be lost.' He then said the only way to get through it was 'to fix it on some one else.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a powerful admission of guilt, indicating he lacks an alibi and is fabricating a story to blame another person, which is exactly what he did in his formal statement.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: M'Carthy admitted he already believed Leary was guilty when he spoke to him. The defense can argue the conversation was misinterpreted or that Leary was speaking hypothetically under duress.

[EVIDENCE ev10_burke_quarrel]
Description: Hyam Barnett, the hatter who sold Clifford his new hat, testified that Clifford 'seemed terrified' of Mary Burke when she entered the shop and that 'they seemed as if they had been quarrelling before they came in.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: This is irrelevant to the actions of the defendant, Leary.
Defense Strength: 0.7
Defense Reasoning: This contradicts Burke's claim that she and Clifford were happy together and introduces the possibility that she had a motive to harm him, supporting Leary's accusation against her.

[EVIDENCE ev12_no_money_found]
Description: When Leary was apprehended at his workplace the day after the murder, he was searched and found to have only an 'eighteen-penny piece' on him. No part of the victim's stolen money was found on his person or in his lodgings.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: Leary could have hidden the money or passed it to an accomplice, such as his wife.
Defense Strength: 0.8
Defense Reasoning: The primary motive for the crime was robbery, yet none of the proceeds were found on the defendant. This significantly weakens the prosecution's case regarding motive.

[EVIDENCE ev13_leary_good_character]
Description: David Helston, Leary's employer, testified that he had a 'good character' with him and described him as a 'quiet, sober, industrious man.'
Prosecution Strength: 0.1
Prosecution Reasoning: A person's general character does not preclude them from committing a specific crime, especially one motivated by a sudden opportunity for wealth.
Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: This suggests that the violent murder is inconsistent with the defendant's known personality and behavior, making his involvement less likely.

[EVIDENCE ev14_burke_hammer]

Prosecution Strength: 0.1

Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: This shows that the prosecution's key witness also possessed a potential weapon, lending credibility to Leary's claim that she was the one who committed the murder with a hammer.

information:
[EVIDENCE ev1]
Description: George Collins, the victim, testified that on the night of April 9th, he fastened his premises securely. He was alerted at 4:30 AM that his property had been broken into, apparently by force using crowbars.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Establishes that a burglary occurred and that the entry was unlawful and forceful, which is a key element of the charge.
Defense Strength: 0.1
Defense Reasoning: This fact does not directly implicate any of the defendants.

[EVIDENCE ev3]
Description: John Woolfe testified that he let a stable in Hoxton to the defendant Thomas Tyler in late April. The key for the stable hung over the gate for common access.
Prosecution Strength: 0.4
Prosecution Reasoning: Links defendant Tyler to a location where stolen goods were allegedly seen and where a stolen skin was later found.
Defense Strength: 0.6
Defense Reasoning: The fact that the key was publicly accessible weakens the exclusive link between Tyler and anything found in the stable, suggesting others could have used it.

[EVIDENCE ev5]
Description: John Wittam, a porter, testified that defendant James Knight gave him three skins on May 7th, asking him to find a buyer and claiming they belonged to a Russian ship.
Prosecution Strength: 0.8
Prosecution Reasoning: Shows James Knight was in possession of the stolen goods and was actively trying to sell them under a false pretense.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: Knight could argue he was merely selling them on behalf of his brother, as he claimed in his defense, and was repeating the story he was told.

[EVIDENCE ev9]
Description: John Pook testified that Jane Stamfield brought three of the stolen skins to his shop to sell. She first claimed her husband brought them from abroad, but when confronted, changed her story to say she received them from an unknown Jew on London Bridge.
Prosecution Strength: 0.9
Prosecution Reasoning: Demonstrates Stamfield's possession of stolen goods and her use of conflicting, implausible stories to explain it, which indicates consciousness of guilt.
Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: Her defense rests on being an innocent party duped into selling stolen goods, but her lies severely undermine this position.

[EVIDENCE ev11]
Description: James Knight's Defense: He claimed he received the skins from his brother Samuel, who told him they came from a Russian captain, and he was merely trying to help sell them.

Defense Strength: 0.2
Defense Reasoning: It attempts to shift the primary blame for knowing the goods were stolen onto his brother Samuel, portraying himself as a less culpable party.

[EVIDENCE ev12]
Description: Samuel Knight's Defense: He claimed a man at a pub who knew a Russian merchant gave him the skins to sell on commission, and he asked his brother James to help find buyers.
Prosecution Strength: 0.2
Prosecution Reasoning: This is a standard, uncorroborated defense for possession of stolen goods. The supposed 'Russian merchant' was never produced or identified.
Defense Strength: 0.3
Defense Reasoning: It provides an alternative, albeit weak, explanation for his possession of the skins that does not involve theft.

Defense Strength: 0.5
Defense Reasoning: Provides direct testimony that James Knight could not have committed the break-in, though it doesn't account for his subsequent possession of the goods.

Defense Reasoning: The testimony provides a character reference and shows Knight had a regular lodging, but it fails as an alibi due to the date discrepancy.

[EVIDENCE ev10]

[EVIDENCE ev12]
